## Fallback models

Each role in `models` takes a list, and the list is tried in order. The step runs on the first model; when
the **provider** fails it, the step moves to the next one:

```json
{
  "models": {
    "hunter.logic": ["opencode:openai/gpt-5", "claude:sonnet-latest"],
    "default": ["claude:sonnet-latest", "claude:opus-latest"]
  }
}
```

A role not listed uses `models.default`, fallbacks included. A list of one model behaves exactly as
before: no fallback, and nothing new is recorded. `--model` names one model, so a run with it has no
fallbacks; the materiality judge keeps its one measured model.

**When it moves.** Only on a failure that is the provider's, not the model's answer, and only after the
model has used its own retries:

| Cause | Moves to the next model? |
| --- | --- |
| `rate_limit`, `quota_exhausted`, `network_transient`, `protocol_truncation`, `watchdog_timeout` (the step timed out), `model_unavailable` | yes |
| `auth_invalid` (the login was refused, "Not logged in") | yes, skipping every later model on the same credential |
| `format_violation` (a bad answer, after its one format retry) | no |
| `context_window_exceeded`, `output_limit_exceeded`, `safety_refusal` | no |
| anything else (configuration, protocol conformance, cancellation, an unconfirmed abort) | no |

"The same credential" is the binding's credential: every Claude model shares the run's one Claude
credential, and an OpenCode model's credential is its provider plus the kind of credential it runs on (a
DeepSeek API key, an OpenAI subscription). So a refused Claude login skips the other Claude models and moves
to an OpenCode model, a refused DeepSeek key skips the other DeepSeek models and moves to another provider,
and the reverse. A cancelled run starts no further model.

**A fenced credential.** A metered attempt whose usage the provider never reported (a timeout, a stream
cut short) fences its credential for the rest of the run, so nothing runs on it blindly: the usage the
platform prices from would have a hole. A
later model on that credential is then refused before any request: it is recorded `skipped`, and the
list goes on to a model on another credential. So a metered OpenCode model that times out moves only to
a model on another credential, never to another model on the same one.

**Time.** Each model gets the step's own retries, each with the step's full timeout, so the longest a step
can take grows with the list: a step whose three models all keep timing out takes three times what one
model would. Only the run's own ceiling bounds the whole step.

**Cost.** The same holds for money: each model's attempts are paid on its own credential, so a step whose
three models all fail after spending can cost up to three times one model. The engine shows no dollar figure
and holds no dollar ceiling; the Crysk platform prices every attempt from the usage the engine reports, and
its limits (Review > Limits in the dashboard) are compared with its estimate before the run, which does not
price fallbacks.

**Checked before anything spends.** Every model of every list is resolved, bound and admitted with the rest
of the plan, before the confirmation, so a fallback that cannot run (no executable, no credential, a
backend not admitted) fails the run up front instead of when its turn comes. OpenCode models may name
several providers, and a free model may sit beside a metered one: each model runs through its own OpenCode
server, projected with only its own credential (see "Several OpenCode providers in one review" below). A
refused login moves past every other model on the same credential to the next one on another. The confirm
menu's free label counts the fallbacks too, so a free first model with a metered fallback is not shown as
free.

**What is recorded.** In `pipeline.json`, a step whose role listed several models has:

- `model`, `route` and `effort_applied` of the model that **ran** (the last one that reached its provider),
  written when the step settles over the first model stamped before the spawn, with its `effort` and, on
  OpenCode, the `variant` it was sent (see [Effort](#effort)).
- `model_attempts`: every model tried, in order, each with its `model`, `route`, `effort`,
  `effort_applied`, `variant` (when one was sent), `status` (`ok`, `failed` or `skipped`), `attempts`, the
  `cause` it failed on and its own `usage_v2`. `skipped` means it never reached its provider: after a
  refused login on its credential (`cause` `auth_invalid`), or with no cause when its credential was fenced
  or it failed before its first request. The step reports the cause and detail of the model that ran.
  Models can bill differently, so the step's `usage_v2` sums them and only these
  entries keep each model's billing.
- `attempts` counts every model's attempts that reached a provider, and attempts are numbered across models, so each model's
  attempt logs and settlement receipts keep their own files; the pointers name the last one.

Spend is reserved per attempt on the binding of the model that runs it, exactly as for a single model.
The per-agent model the platform report carries, and the provider and model named for a failed hunter,
are the ones that ran. A step with one model records exactly what it recorded before.

## Effort

How hard a model works is set per step with the Claude CLI's `--effort` control, and **Crysk owns it**:
every Claude Code step is spawned with an explicit `--effort <level>`, never the CLI's implicit default.
That default is `high`, except on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5, where it is `medium`, so leaving it implicit
meant a model alias moving to a new release could silently change how deeply a step explores.

An agent prompt may declare its own level in its frontmatter, beside `model:`:

```yaml
---
name: my-hunter
model: sonnet
effort: xhigh
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
```

The levels are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. Anything else fails at preflight and names the
file. When a prompt omits `effort:`, the engine supplies a default for the step's role, so a custom or lab
prompt set still runs at an explicit level:

| Role | Default | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hunter | `xhigh` | Measured on a real 280-line PR (Sonnet 5.5, 4 hunters x 2 replicates): `medium` found something in 0 of 8 runs, `high` in 6 of 8, `xhigh` in 8 of 8 and all 4 known bugs, `max` in 7 of 8 at about four times the wall time. |
| Refuter | `high` | `medium` refuted a pre-labeled known blocker in 3 of 4 verdicts on real findings, which deletes it; `high` kept it as latent in 3 of 4. |
| Summarizer, rereview verifier | `high` | Unmeasured, so they keep what every model ran at before the 5.5 family. |

The bundled prompts declare `effort: xhigh` on the hunters and `effort: high` on the refuter. The rereview
verifier runs as the refuter's agent, so it follows the refuter's frontmatter for model, effort and tools.
What it is told is the engine's own text, not the refuter's: it answers whether an earlier finding's defect is
still present at the current head, which is not the refuter's question. A custom `review-refuter.md` therefore
no longer changes the verifier's instructions, only its model, effort and tools. There is no CLI flag or
environment variable that overrides effort, and the child process never inherits `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`
from your shell. `xhigh` hunters cost roughly three times what `high` did per hunter, measured on past runs; the
engine prints no estimate, and the Crysk platform shows what a review actually cost.

**Consolidation.** After the refuter, one more step reads the findings about to be posted and rewrites the
list so each comment states one defect: findings
…[仅保留首 16KB/中段 8KB/末 8KB]…
ch is what lets the platform report API and
  subscription use apart.
- **Closed when done.** A server stops when its last step ends, whether it succeeded, failed or was
  cancelled, and any server still up stops when the run ends.

A plan on a single OpenCode credential behaves exactly as before.

### claude-code: one credential per run, in the order you choose

A run uses exactly **one** Claude credential, chosen once when it starts and never switched mid-run. Set
the order in your person config (`~/.crysk/config.json`; a repository file cannot set it; in CI, the
`CRYSK_CREDENTIALS` variable passed as the action's `credentials` input):

```json
{ "credentials": { "claude": ["subscription", "api_key"] } }
```

- `subscription` is the Claude Code subscription: the `CRYSK_CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`
  variable (`claude setup-token`), or a login on this machine (the macOS Keychain item, or
  `~/.claude/.credentials.json`).
- `api_key` is an Anthropic API key, billed per token: `CRYSK_CLAUDE_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

The run uses the first credential in the list that is set. A credential that is set but not listed is never
used. If none of the listed ones is set and the plan sends a step to the Claude CLI, the review stops before
it spends anything, with a message that names the order and what is set. A plan with no Claude step ignores
Claude credentials. A dry run never stops for this: it authenticates nothing.

**The default, when `credentials` is absent, is `["subscription", "api_key"]`.** This is a billing change
for anyone who has both a subscription and an API key: before, the Claude CLI preferred the key whenever
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` was set and the review billed per token; now the subscription runs and the key is not
used. Put `api_key` first to keep billing per token. With only one of them set, nothing changes.

The Claude child sees only the chosen credential, under the CLI's own name: `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` for the
subscription, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for the key. The other one, and `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, are removed from its
environment. `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` is not a credential Crysk chooses: put an API key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
instead. How a run bills follows the choice: on the API key it is metered, so the platform's dollar limits can
skip it; on the subscription it draws on quota and is never skipped for cost.

On macOS with `/usr/bin/security` present, a run on the subscription projects the Keychain OAuth record into
the child. A run on the API key attaches no Keychain broker at all. If the `Claude Code-credentials` item is
absent entirely, projection fails closed and the step does not run. If the Keychain item exists but the CLI
moved its OAuth record out of the expected shape, projection degrades (`#279`) and the child runs on the
run's own environment, which holds no API key on a subscription run, so it never bills a key the run did not
choose: it runs on whatever the Claude CLI's own credential store holds, and fails only if that is empty too.

## Verifying at $0

### `crysk config`

```
$ crysk config
  repo   <repo>/.crysk/config.json (absent)
  global ~/.crysk/config.json (present)

  agents_dir                default (unset)
  ...
  models                    global default=claude:sonnet-latest,
                            hunter.logic=opencode:deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash,claude:opus-latest
                            (effort high)
  credentials               global  claude=subscription,api_key
  max_changed_lines         global  3000
  post                      global  true
  ...

  repo beats global, except on a capped key — there the NARROWER value wins, so
  a committed file can spend less of your money but never more. capped means the
  repo asked for the wider value and the global ceiling took it away; default
  means neither file named the key, and the resolver's own fallback decides at
  run time.
```

### `crysk doctor`

The exact-binding probe: which binary, which credential kind, whether its projection is ready, and
what isolation actually holds — not a generic "is claude installed" check. Its Claude check applies the rule
a run chooses by: a `CRYSK_CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `CRYSK_CLAUDE_API_KEY` variable first, then the CLI's own
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, then this machine's login (`~/.claude/.credentials.json`,
or on macOS the Keychain broker). `~/.claude.json` or `~/.claude/session.json` alone no longer count, and
neither does `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`; the hint names `CRYSK_CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (from `claude setup-token`)
and `CRYSK_CLAUDE_API_KEY`.

The Claude CLI blocks only when the configuration sends some step to it: no `models`, or any role, fallback
or judge (with `materiality_gate` on) that resolves to a `claude:` model. When every step, fallbacks
included, resolves to an `opencode:` model (`models.default` covers the roles you do not list), a missing or signed-out Claude CLI is listed as not needed, and the probe
checks only the OpenCode routes.

```
$ crysk doctor
  [✓] claude: Claude Code CLI is installed and authenticated (2.1.281 (Claude Code))
  [!] provider:codegraph_policy_unenforced: no dedicated codegraph sensitive-file policy is
      enforced yet; isolation relies on --strict-mcp-config with a codegraph-only mcp.json
  ...
Environment is operational, but some optional tools or configurations are degraded.
```

### `crysk review --dry-run` — two caveats

- **In PR mode it returns before route admission.** `crysk review --pr <n> --dry-run` prints the
  plan from the diff and the config alone, before any credential is projected or
  route bound, so a plan that would die immediately at admission (an OpenCode effort the model does not
  offer, a fallback with no executable) can still print a clean dry-run. Local dry-run resolves the
  route plan and admission first (`#120`), so it catches admission refusals. Neither stops for a missing
  Claude credential: a dry run authenticates nothing.
- **The plan shows no cost.** The engine computes no dollar figure, so neither the plan nor the confirmation
  prints a cost range; the Crysk platform shows what a review cost. A platform run's dollar limits are
  applied by the CI run step (see [GitHub Actions](github-actions.md#spend-controls)).

## What is proven for OpenCode, and what is not

OpenCode has completed real, end-to-end reviews — not a mock, not a fixture — but on narrow slices,
each ledgered live with real cost accounted:

- A subscription-style smoke (`#116`): one provider, one model, a 7-line diff, three hunters. All
  six conformance axes (auth, tools/MCP, terminal, usage, cleanup, provenance) verified live, at
  $0.00 cash. The refuter, scout, summarizer, parity hunter and codegraph/MCP integration were **not**
  exercised.
- The refuter on OpenCode (`#142`, item 1): closed — it ran, found the planted defect, and typed it
  correctly. It also returned `inconclusive` on a deterministic, 0-hop finding with two fabricated
  file citations — a real gap, but in `proof_refs` validation generally, not specific to OpenCode.
- A metered provider (`deepseek`) ran a real self-review at $0.06 and found a real issue the Claude
  arm on the same diff missed.
- A `provider_free` route completed a full PR-sized review (20 files, +365/−1987) at $0, wiring
  proven end to end — but it did roughly 1/17th the reading (input tokens) of a Claude control arm
  on the same diff and reported the same "nothing found" answer, which is weak evidence on a diff
  with no planted defect, not proof of equivalent quality.
- `zai` is code-path-identical to the proven `deepseek` route but unrun — no credential was
  available to prove it. `zai-coding-plan` (a flat-fee plan behind an API key) is priced `$0` by
  OpenCode's catalog, so it runs as `provider_free` with its own `auth.json` key projected
  (`#280`) — verified in code and tests, not in a live run.
- Codegraph/MCP integration on a target that actually has an index, and a fully parity-hunter- and
  scout-exercised run, remain unverified.

OpenCode is not a default backend. Treat it as proven for the slices above and unproven elsewhere.

# GitHub Actions Integration

> **The maintained user docs are on [crysk.dev/docs](https://crysk.dev/docs/)** (index for agents:
> [crysk.dev/llms.txt](https://crysk.dev/llms.txt)). Start with the
> [Quickstart](https://crysk.dev/docs/quickstart-github-actions/), and use the
> [Action reference](https://crysk.dev/docs/github-actions/action-reference/) and the
> [error codes](https://crysk.dev/docs/reference/error-codes/). This file is the engine's longer CI guide. It
> stays because tests and links already posted on pull requests point at its sections and error-code anchors,
> and the site is the source for anything that differs.

Crysk reviews every pull request automatically: a multi-agent hunt with adversarial refutation runs
inside a GitHub Actions job, posts findings as PR comments, and writes a step summary. Its commit status
(`crysk`; the legacy `pr-hero` status is no longer posted, so a branch-protection rule on it must move to `crysk`) is a gate by default: blocking findings turn it red, so
require `crysk` in branch protection to block a merge on them. `mode: advisory` keeps it green. See [Gate mode](#gate-mode-the-status-is-the-check).

## Quick path

1. **Add one Claude secret** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret):
   `CRYSK_CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (your Claude subscription, from `claude setup-token`) or
   `CRYSK_CLAUDE_API_KEY` (an Anthropic API key, billed per token). One is enough. With both set, a run
   uses the subscription unless `credentials.claude` puts `api_key` first (see
   [Configuration, Credentials](configuration.md#credentials)). That is today's Claude CI; for OpenCode
   models, see the end of this list.
2. **Add the one workflow file.** Copy the YAML under [What the workflow does](#what-the-workflow-does)
   to `.github/workflows/crysk.yml`, or run `npx -y crysk setup --ci` (or `crysk ci init`) in a clone of
   your repo, which writes the same template (`uses: cryskai/crysk@v0`). You do not need Crysk
   installed locally: the file is the whole install. The command also checks the GitHub CLI: if `gh` is
   missing or logged out, it prints why the CI loop needs it (`gh secret set`, `crysk status`,
   `crysk triage reply`) and how to fix it, and in a terminal it offers to install it (macOS with
   Homebrew) and to run `gh auth login`; the workflow is written either way. Its next steps print the
   `gh secret set` and `gh variable set` commands for your setup (see [`crysk ci init`](#scaffolding-with-crysk-ci-init)).
   It reviews every push to a pull request, answers a
   `/crysk review` comment (see [Re-review on demand](#re-review-on-demand)), and answers a
   `/crysk override` comment (see [Overriding a red gate](#overriding-a-red-gate)). Do **not** copy this
   repository's own `.github/workflows/crysk.yml`: that file is generated with
   `OWN_CI_WORKFLOW_OPTIONS` so this repo can dogfood the checkout (`uses: ./`,
   `max-changed-lines: 5000`, and a step that pins the pull request head on a comment run).
   `test/packaging.test.ts` asserts each file against its own generator options; it does **not** assert
   the two are byte-identical. The template names every `CRYSK_*` secret it can pass; a secret your
   repository does not have arrives empty and counts as absent, so a Claude-only repository keeps every line.
3. **Write the repository review instructions (optional, recommended).** Put a `REVIEW.md` at the
   repository root (the file name Claude Code Review uses) with the facts a reviewer cannot infer from
   the diff: a deliberate oddity that looks like a bug, an invariant enforced outside the diff, an
   ownership rule a newcomer would break. `npx -y crysk init` scaffolds one when the repo has no
   instructions yet: replace its placeholder lines and delete the `human-attention-required` marker
   line. A repo that already has `.crysk/gotchas.md` can keep it: without a `REVIEW.md`, Crysk reads
   that instead. The hunters and the refuter read the file as facts about the codebase; with
   `materiality_gate` on, the materiality judge also applies its "Not blocking here" rules to blocking
   findings, only for style, naming, test hygiene, generated code and dev scripts (never to logic,
   correctness, data, contract or security findings). With neither file the review runs on the default guidance; a file that exists
   but is empty or still the scaffold fails the run with [`CRYSK-GOTCHAS-MISSING`](#crysk-gotchas-missing).
4. **Commit the file to the default branch.** Comment-triggered runs read the base branch, so the file
   must be there, not only on your feature branch.
5. **Require the check.** In branch protection, require the `crysk` status check (the gate). The legacy `pr-hero` status is no longer posted, so a repository that still requires it is blocked until the rule moves to `crysk`. Do not require the
   `review` job, which stays green even when it finds blocking issues. A private repository on GitHub Free
   cannot require status checks (GitHub returns HTTP 403), so there the gate is advisory in practice.
6. **Open a pull request** from a branch in this repository (not a fork). Crysk comments inline, posts
   a summary review, and writes a `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` block within a few minutes. If no credential
   secret is set, the run fails red and its step summary lists the commands that set one.
7. **Verify readiness any time** with `crysk doctor` — locally it checks for the workflow file's presence.

To pick the models each step runs on (OpenCode models included, as primary or fallback), set them per role
in the `CRYSK_MODELS` repository variable and add each OpenCode provider's `CRYSK_OPENCODE_*` secret — see
[OpenCode in CI](#opencode-in-ci). You do not need a different Action.

**Upgrading a workflow from before the `CRYSK_*` secrets.** The `anthropic-api-key`, `claude-token`,
`opencode-auth` and `routing` inputs are removed: a workflow that still passes a value in one stops at the
trigger with [`CRYSK-INPUT-REMOVED`](#crysk-input-removed), before anything is installed. Re-run
`npx -y crysk ci init --force` (it rewrites the workflow and prints the commands for the new secrets and
variables), or replace those lines by hand with the `crysk-secrets`, `models` and `credentials` lines of the
template, and set the [`CRYSK_*` secrets](#crysk_-secrets).

## What the workflow does

```yaml
name: Crysk Review

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]
  issue_comment: # `/crysk review` — read from the default branch's copy of this file
    types: [created]

permissions:
  actions: read # admission gate lists this workflow's past runs
  contents: read # actions/checkout
  pull-requests: write # inline comments + review + step summary
  issues: write # resolving/replying on review threads (GitHub models PR conversations as issues)
  statuses: write # commit status updates
  checks: write # admission attempt ledger

jobs:
  review:
    # Same-repo pushes, and comments that start with `/crysk review`, `/crysk recheck` or `/crysk override`. Never reads secrets.
    if: >-
      (github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository) ||
      (github.event_name == 'issue_comment' && github.event.issue.pull_request && startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/crysk review')) ||
      (github.event_name == 'issue_comment' && github.event.issue.pull_request && startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/crysk recheck')) ||
      (github.event_name == 'issue_comment' && github.event.issue.pull_request && startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/crysk override'))
    concurrency:
      group: ${{ ((github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository) || (startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/crysk review') && contains(fromJSON('["OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association)) || (startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/crysk recheck') && contains(fromJSON('["OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association)) || (startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/crysk override') && contains(fromJSON('["OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association))) && format('pr-hero-review-{0}', github.event.pull_request.number || github.event.issue.number) || format('pr-hero-noop-{0}', github.run_id) }}
      cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0 # see "Why fetch-depth: 0" below
      - name: Run Crysk
        id: pr-hero
        uses: cryskai/crysk@v0
        with:
          github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          crysk-secrets: |
            CRYSK_CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN=${{ secrets.CRYSK_CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN }}
            CRYSK_CLAUDE_API_KEY=${{ secrets.CRYSK_CLAUDE_API_KEY }}
            CRYSK_OPENCODE_OPENAI_OAUTH=${{ secrets.CRYSK_OPENCODE_OPENAI_OAUTH }}
            CRYSK_OPENCODE_${{ fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[0] }}_API_KEY=${{ secrets[format('CRYSK_OPENCODE_{0}_API_KEY', fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[0])] }}
            CRYSK_OPENCODE_${{ fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[1] }}_API_KEY=${{ secrets[format('CRYSK_OPENCODE_{0}_API_KEY', fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[1])] }}
            CRYSK_OPENCODE_${{ fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[2] }}_API_KEY=${{ secrets[format('CRYSK_OPENCODE_{0}_API_KEY', fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[2])] }}
            CRYSK_OPENCODE_${{ fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[3] }}_API_KEY=${{ secrets[format('CRYSK_OPENCODE_{0}_API_KEY', fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[3])] }}
            CRYSK_OPENCODE_${{ fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[4] }}_API_KEY=${{ secrets[format('CRYSK_OPENCODE_{0}_API_KEY', fromJSON(vars.CRYSK_OPENCODE_PROVIDERS || '[]')[4])] }}
          models: ${{ vars.CRYSK_MODELS }}
          credentials: ${{ vars.CRYSK_CREDENTIALS }}
          profile: ${{ vars.CRYSK_PROFILE }}
          mode: gate
```

`crysk setup --ci` generates this file, with comments explaining each piece — see
`generateCiWorkflowTemplate` in `src/ci/setup.ts`. It writes `.github/workflows/crysk.yml`, unless the
repository already has the pre-rename `.github/workflows/pr-hero.yml`: that file stays where it is, and
`--force` rewrites it in place (no `crysk.yml` appears beside it, because two workflow files would review
every pull request twice; if both exist, setup refuses to write either and `crysk doctor` reports it).
It refuses to overwrite a customized workflow unless you pass `--force`, and it never touches a
`pr-hero-force.yml` scaffolded by an older version (that file keeps working; you can delete it once this
one is on your default branch). The name of the file does not matter to Crysk, so you can also keep
`pr-hero.yml` for good or rename it to `crysk.yml` yourself.

**Upgrading from the `/pr-hero` commands.** The commands are now `/crysk review`, `/crysk review --full`,
`/crysk recheck`, `/crysk override` and `/crysk stop`. The `/pr-hero …` spellings are no longer
commands: a comment that uses them starts nothing. A workflow file scaffolded earlier only starts a run on
`/pr-hero …` comments, so no comment starts a run there: re-run `crysk ci init --force` (or copy the `if:`
and `group:` lines above) to accept `/crysk …`.

The action does the rest: it checks that a credential is set (and fails the run red, with the commands
that fix it, when none is), parses a `/crysk review` comment and checks that its author has write
access, resolves the pull request and its head commit from the event, and uploads the run directory
(see [Triaging a CI review](#triaging-a-ci-review)).

Three choices in the job are load-bearing:

- **Concurrency is per job and keyed on the pull request number.** A workflow-level group keyed on
  `github.head_ref || github.ref` would put every comment on every pull request into one group, because
  `head_ref` is empty on `issue_comment`, so any comment could cancel any in-flight review. A fork's
  push, a comment that does not start with `/crysk review`, and a comment whose author GitHub does not
  associate with the repository as `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR` each get a unique group, so
  those jobs never cancel or replace a review.
- **Only a new push cancels.** The `if:` filter is a prefix, so a near-miss comment ("/crysk review
  please") from an associated author lands in the pull request's group too; cancelling there would kill
  a paid review in flight before the action ignores the comment. A comment run queues instead. A push
  never waits: it cancels whatever is running, a forced review included, because that head is gone;
  comment again on the new head. GitHub keeps one *pending* run per group and a newer run replaces it,
  which is why a stranger's comment never enters the group: it could otherwise replace a maintainer's
  queued review with a run the action then refuses. Known gap: an associated author's later comment (a
  writer's near-miss or second real command, or a read-only member's or collaborator's refused one)
  still replaces a comment run already waiting behind a running review, and `--full` followed by a plain
  `/crysk review` loses the `--full`. Comment again to recover. The job `if:` does not check the
  association, so a writer GitHub reports under another one (a private org member shown as
  `CONTRIBUTOR`) still gets a review, because the action checks the real permission, but in its own
  group, unserialized beside a review already running.
- **Fork pushes are skipped.** GitHub gives fork `pull_request` runs no secrets. A maintainer comments
  `/crysk review` instead; see [Fork pull requests](#fork-pull-requests).

Keep every `with:` line even when you only use Claude: an unset secret or variable expands to empty,
which the Action treats as absent. Deleting the line for the credential you *did* set is what breaks. An
unused provider slot renders as `CRYSK_OPENCODE__API_KEY=` and is skipped.

**A run that cannot start the review still says so on the pull request.** When there is no
model credential, the pull request number or head cannot be resolved, the commenter's permission
cannot be verified, or an install step fails before Crysk starts, Crysk posts one `crysk`
commit status (`error`) and one comment on the pull request. A review that starts and then fails also
does, when the CLI reports an error or every review hunter fails; if the CLI takes the review's lock and then
stops before it reports an outcome, Crysk posts the comment, and its `error` status on the head that lock is on, when that head's `crysk` status is still `pending` or cannot be read. A review cancelled mid-review sets `error` `CRYSK-CANCELLED: not reviewed — /crysk review reviews this head` on its head, so a cancelled gate never stays pending. The `pending` status names its run: in Actions it links to that run's attempt, so the status's link opens the Actions run, and a cancel settles only the pending that names its own run. A `pending` from an older pr-hero, with no run link, is matched by its creation time instead. Without a readable record of the lock, pr-hero posts the comment alone, with no status. A settled status (`success`, `error` or `failure`) stays as the CLI left it. The comment gives the error code, whose fix it is (your configuration, a provider, pr-hero,
or unclassified) and the command that fixes it.
A newer comment replaces the older one from the same author. Crysk removes its earlier outcome comment once a later run has completed a review. A denied or ignored `/crysk review`
comment posts no comment: the trigger reacts to it instead ([Reactions on a command](#reactions-on-a-command)). A review that ran keeps its own status. A size or limits skip sets a `failure`
status in gate mode and none in advisory (see [Gate mode](#gate-mode-the-status-is-the-check)).

### Scaffolding with `crysk ci init`

`crysk ci init` (the same as `crysk setup --ci`) writes the workflow above and, in its next steps, prints the
commands that put your setup where the workflow reads it. It reads your person config
(`~/.crysk/config.json`) first, and prints, never ru
…[文件过长——中段 8KB 抽样]…
 such as an agent's signature, are ignored, and so is
whitespace at the end of the line. Leading whitespace means no job starts at all. Other words on that line,
as in `/crysk review please`, start a job that ends without reviewing. The commenter needs write access to
the repository; a comment from anyone else is refused. `gh run rerun` on a skipped run re-evaluates the gates
and does not force.

A local agent (Claude Code) posts the same comment:

```bash
gh pr comment <number> --body "/crysk review"
```

It must not run `crysk review --pr <n> --force` when the goal is a CI review.

The comment run passes `--force`. That bypasses the size gate, admission, and the platform's limits for
that run only. It does not reset the durable ledger. An empty effective diff (everything excluded)
still does not review.

`--force` never widens discovery. A re-review only hunts the commits since the last completed review,
and that review is identified by the summary marker it posted for its head commit. So when a prior
review of the **same head** was hollow or wrong (for example, its hunters returned nothing), every
later run on that head reports "No changes to discover" and runs no hunter. Recover with `--full`,
which re-discovers the whole pull request range:

```text
/crysk review --full
```

Prior findings are still verified and triaged as usual; only discovery widens.

**Fork pull requests** are reviewed only this way: their own pushes are skipped, and a maintainer's
comment runs the review in the base repository's context (see
[Fork pull requests](#fork-pull-requests)).

**Workflows scaffolded before the comment trigger** have no `issue_comment` listener, so a comment does
nothing there. They have a dispatch-only `.github/workflows/pr-hero-force.yml` instead, which still
works because the action keeps the `pr-number`, `force`, and `full` inputs it sets:

```bash
gh workflow run pr-hero-force.yml -f pr=<number>              # force
gh workflow run pr-hero-force.yml -f pr=<number> -f full=true # force and re-discover
```

Re-scaffold with `crysk ci init --force` to switch to the comment trigger. It rewrites
the review workflow only (`pr-hero.yml` or `crysk.yml`, whichever the repository has) and leaves
`pr-hero-force.yml` in place; delete that file yourself once the new workflow is on the default branch.

This repository is reviewed through the Crysk platform, which configures its review, so it commits no
`crysk.yml` or `.crysk/config.json` of its own. `OWN_CI_WORKFLOW_OPTIONS` still generates the workflow
it used before: on a comment a first step resolves the PR head commit and checkout pins that commit
before `uses: ./`, so a comment run reviews with the pull request's own engine rather than the default
branch's. Consumer workflows run the published `cryskai/crysk@v0`, where the checkout does not select
the engine.

- **When it takes effect.** GitHub reads a comment-triggered workflow from the default branch, so the
  comment trigger works only once the workflow (`crysk.yml`, or `pr-hero.yml` in a repository set up before
  the rename) with its `issue_comment` trigger is on the default
  branch (for example `main`, not an integration branch like `dev`). Until then a comment starts nothing. In a
  consumer repository, the comment handling also needs an action release that has it, reached through
  the `@v0` tag the workflow pins.
- **Minimum action version.** This workflow listens to comments, and only an action release that ships
  the comment handling checks the command and the commenter's write access. An older action reviews on
  ANY comment that starts with `/crysk review`, from anyone who can comment, with your secrets. Do
  not pair this workflow with an action older than the release that adds it: if you pin a tag or a
  commit sha instead of `@v0`, pin one at or after that release.
- **Older heads (this repository).** The comment run loads the PR head's own `action.yml`, so on a head
  from before the comment handling existed the run reviews without reading the comment: no `--force`
  and no `--full`. Merge or rebase the PR onto a base that has it first.
- **Trust (this repository).** A comment run here runs the PR head's code, including its
  `bun install`, with the workflow's secrets. So the commenter's write access is checked twice: by the
  workflow's own pre-checkout step, before any of the head's code runs, and again by the head's
  `action.yml`. The first check fails closed, so an old branch whose `action.yml` predates the check
  still refuses a commenter without write access.

### Check Runs ledger

Admission attempts are persisted as Check Runs named `crysk/ci-admission` on the reviewed commit (a commit
first reviewed by an older release holds them under `pr-hero/ci-admission`, which Crysk still reads, so the
attempt count carries over).
The workflow needs **`checks: write`** (listed under [Token permissions](#token-permissions)) so Crysk can
reserve attempts before provider spend and record outcomes. PR comments remain presentation only; the
Check Run ledger is authoritative.

An attempt counts toward `ci_max_attempts` when its run reached the provider (completed, failed, or
still in progress) or when admission itself skipped it. Two outcomes spend nothing and do not count: a
run that stood down for a review already in flight on the same head, and a run the size gate or the
platform's limits skipped before any agent started. A run where every hunter stopped on the same rejected credential or spent usage limit does not count either: it reviewed nothing, and nothing in the pull request caused it. A run that stopped on a configuration error (a bad gotchas file or prompt set) before it reviewed anything spends nothing either, and so do forced comment runs (`/crysk review`, `/crysk recheck`): the budget bounds automatic reviews, and a deliberate comment is a spend outside it. A cancelled row does not count either, but it is not
proof that nothing was spent: a cancel signal can arrive after the provider started, so a run that
GitHub concludes as `failure` (for example one killed by `timeout-minutes`) still counts. A skipped run
still shows as a skipped check on the commit.

Skipped and manual-required outcomes include admission metadata in the step summary: decision, reason,
current head, reviewed head, risk class, score, attempt count, remaining budget, policy mode, and a
short policy hash.

## Gate mode: the status is the check

The `crysk` commit status is the check you require in branch protection. The legacy `pr-hero` context is
no longer written, so a repository that still requires `pr-hero` is blocked until the rule moves to `crysk`.
Readers (the admission gate, `crysk status`, the override check) still treat the two as one gate and take the
newest row across both, so a head reviewed earlier keeps its verdict, and an override posted by an older action
only on `pr-hero` still wins. Descriptions are written `crysk: …`
and read in both spellings. The job's exit code does not
carry the review's findings: a finished review exits `0` even when it finds blocking-tier issues. Findings
are published as comments and a summary, and the commit status decides the gate. The exit code does carry
whether the review finished: an incomplete one (a hunter, the refuter, verify, adjudicate or the time ceiling
failed) exits `3` and the job goes red, in gate and advisory mode alike; `/crysk review` runs it again. The
full table is in the README's "Exit codes" section.

The action's `mode` input picks what the status says. It defaults to `gate`:

- **`gate`** (the default): a finished review with blocking findings sets `failure`. A size or limits
  skip also sets `failure`, so an unreviewed head cannot read as a clean one. A clean review, or one with
  only advisory findings, sets `success`.
- **`advisory`**: the status is `success` for every finished review, whatever it finds. This is the
  posture Crysk had before the gate. Skipped reviews post no status, as before.

Either way, a crash, a failed session and a missing findings count set `error`, which is a red check too.

| Cause | `gate`

Why:** the subscription refuses requests until its usage window resets, so an immediate retry would fail the same way

Every failed hunter ran on the OpenAI subscription record, `CRYSK_OPENCODE_OPENAI_OAUTH`.

**Fix:**

Re-run after the limit resets:

```bash
gh pr comment {pr} --body "/crysk review"
```

On a workflow set up before the rename, comment `/crysk review` instead.

Or bill per token: set CRYSK_OPENCODE_OPENAI_API_KEY and stop passing {secret} in the crysk-secrets input (the subscription is used while it is passed):


<a id="prh-provider-unavailable"></a>

### CRYSK-PROVIDER-UNAVAILABLE

**Owner:** provider

**What:** unreachable

**Why:** the request did not complete, and the provider's outcome cannot be confirmed from here

**Fix:**

Re-run the workflow:

```bash
gh run rerun {runId}
```

<a id="prh-provider-refused"></a>

### CRYSK-PROVIDER-REFUSED

**Owner:** provider

**What:** the request was refused

**Why:** the provider's safety system declined this input

**Fix:**

Ask for a new review once:

```bash
gh pr comment {pr} --body "/crysk review"
```

On a workflow set up before the rename, comment `/crysk review` instead.

If it repeats, report it.

<a id="prh-engine-defect"></a>

### CRYSK-ENGINE-DEFECT

**Owner:** Crysk

**What:** Crysk hit an internal error ({detail}) in {step}

**Why:** this is a defect in Crysk, not in your configuration

**Fix:**

Report it, with this run:

```bash
gh issue create -R cryskai/crysk --title "CRYSK-ENGINE-DEFECT {detail}" --body "{runUrl}"
```

<a id="prh-hunters-failed"></a>

### CRYSK-HUNTERS-FAILED

**Owner:** unclassified

**What:** Every hunter failed in {step}: {detail}

**Why:** no hunter returned a result, so there is no finding to report

When every failed hunter reports the same one-line reason from the provider (a transient overload, say: `Anthropic API: Overloaded (HTTP 529)`), it replaces the generic reason after the colon, cut to fit the 140-character status description. A shared `quota_exhausted` cause renders `CRYSK-PROVIDER-LIMITED` instead, with the same words. A shared `auth_invalid` cause renders `CRYSK-CRED-REJECTED` when the record names the secret the hunters ran on and the provider; without them it keeps this code.

When every failed hunter shares a `model_unavailable` cause with its provider known, the run renders `CRYSK-MODEL-UNAVAILABLE` instead; when every failed hunter shares a `missing_provider_record` cause with its provider and model known, it renders `CRYSK-CRED-UNUSABLE`. Any other cause, a missing provider or model, a mix of causes, a hunter with no cause, or a `runtime_unavailable` cause keeps this code.

**Fix:**

Re-run the failed jobs:

```bash
gh run rerun {runId} --failed
```

If it repeats, report it.

#### `context_window_exceeded`

**Why:** the review input is too large for the model, so every hunter was refused and a re-run would send the same request

Every failed hunter shares the `context_window_exceeded` cause (the Claude CLI reports a prompt that is too long, or a request over the size limit, this way).

**Fix:**

Lower `max-changed-lines` in the workflow's `with:` block (or `max_changed_lines` in the repo config), or exclude paths in `.cryskignore` (`.prheroignore` in a repo set up before the rename), then ask for a new review:

```bash
gh pr comment {pr} --body "/crysk review"
```

On a workflow set up before the rename, comment `/crysk review` instead.

<a id="prh-unclassified"></a>

### CRYSK-UNCLASSIFIED

**Owner:** unclassified

**What:** Crysk stopped at {step} and could not tell why

**Why:** rather than guess, it reports this honestly

**Fix:**

Re-run the failed jobs:

```bash
gh run rerun {runId} --failed
```

If it repeats, read the log and report it:

```bash
gh run view {runId} --log-failed
```

#### `github`

**What:** GitHub returned {detail} at {step}, and Crysk cannot tell whose fix it is

**Why:** Crysk does not map this GitHub status to an owner, so it does not guess

**Fix:**

Re-run the failed jobs:

```bash
gh run rerun {runId} --failed
```

If it repeats, read the log and report it:

```bash
gh run view {runId} --log-failed
```

<a id="prh-cancelled"></a>

### CRYSK-CANCELLED

**Owner:** unclassified

**Shown as:** `Not reviewed:`, as a notice rather than an error

**What:** The review was cancelled or superseded by a newer push

**Why:** a newer run replaces this one, so this result would describe an outdated head

**Fix:**

Ask for a review of the current head:

```bash
gh pr comment {pr} --body "/crysk review"
```

On a workflow set up before the rename, comment `/crysk review` instead.

## Troubleshooting

- **`crysk doctor`** locally reports whether `.github/workflows/crysk.yml` (or the pre-rename
  `pr-hero.yml`) exists, and is degraded if both do; inside Actions it
  reports whether the required secrets (or OpenCode auth file) are present (never their values).
- **The review was skipped** (size, limits, or admission) — comment `/crysk review` on the pull
  request. `gh run rerun` on the workflow re-evaluates the gates and skips again. On a workflow
  scaffolded before the comment trigger, run `gh workflow run pr-hero-force.yml -f pr=<n>` instead.
- **A `/crysk review` comment did nothing** — the comment trigger reads the workflow file from the
  default branch, so it works only once that file (with its `issue_comment` trigger) is merged there.
  The comment's first line must be exactly `/crysk review` or `/crysk review --full`, and its author needs
  write access to the repository. An older workflow file has no comment trigger at all: re-scaffold
  with `crysk ci init --force`.
- **The run is red and names a missing credential** — no `CRYSK_*` secret in the `crysk-secrets` input
  has a value. The step summary lists the `gh secret set` commands; adding a secret does not re-run past
  workflows, so re-run that run afterwards.
- **The run is red with `CRYSK-INPUT-REMOVED`** — the workflow still passes a value in a removed input
  (`anthropic-api-key`, `claude-token`, `opencode-auth`, `routing`). Re-run `npx -y crysk ci init --force`,
  or delete those lines and pass the `CRYSK_*` secrets in `crysk-secrets` and the models in `models`.
- **The run is red with `CRYSK-CONFIG-INVALID` naming the `models` or `credentials` input** — the
  `CRYSK_MODELS` or `CRYSK_CREDENTIALS` variable is not valid JSON or breaks a rule. The step's log names
  the entry; run the same object through `crysk config` locally (in `~/.crysk/config.json`) to see the
  message, then set the variable again.
- **Every re-run says "No changes to discover" after a hollow review** — a prior review of the same
  head completed without really reviewing (for example, every hunter returned nothing within
  seconds), and its summary marker now scopes discovery to nothing. On a head that was genuinely
  reviewed this message is expected and needs no action. Otherwise, comment `/crysk review --full`
  to re-discover the whole pull request; see [Re-review on demand](#re-review-on-demand).
- **No comment appears on the PR** — check `permissions: pull-requests: write` is present, and that at
  least one `CRYSK_*` secret is set and passed in `crysk-secrets`. Fork pushes never receive those
  secrets; a maintainer's `/crysk review` comment reviews them.
- **The review job is red** — never because of findings. Read `status` and the exit code to tell the causes
  apart: `error` is a fatal failure and the `::error::` annotation in the log names it; an **empty** `status`
  means every hunter died (the log shows their failures); `reviewed` with exit `3` means the review is
  incomplete (a hunter, the refuter, verify, adjudicate or the time ceiling failed) and `/crysk review`
  retries it; `reviewed` with exit `1` means some comments could not be posted, or no reviewer ran. See "Gate mode" above. An OpenCode model whose provider has no
  `CRYSK_OPENCODE_*` secret fails closed rather than skipping.

# Release Runbook

This document is the operational runbook for releasing new versions of Crysk (npm package `crysk`, GitHub repository `cryskai/crysk`; the package was called `pr-hero` before the rename, see Step 4c). It covers the repository branching model, versioning rules, step-by-step release instructions, CI/CD pipeline automation, post-release verification, and rollback procedures.

---

## 1. Branching Model & Commit Standards

Crysk uses **Trunk-Based Development** centered on the `main` branch:

- **Primary Branch (`main`)**: The stable source of truth. All releases are tagged directly from `main`.
- **Feature & Fix Branches**: Work happens in short-lived branches branched off `main` (e.g. `feat/new-hunter`, `fix/tui-wrap`, `chore/bump-deps`).
- **Pull Request Gating**: Branches merge into `main` via pull requests only after passing automated CI checks (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`: test suite, type checking, linter check, and binary compilation).
- **Conventional Commits**: Commit messages follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) specification:
  - `feat:` New user-facing features or capabilities
  - `fix:` Bug fixes and defect corrections
  - `chore:` Toolchain updates, dependency bumps, maintenance
  - `chore(release):` Release commits bumping versions and changelog
  - `docs:` Documentation improvements
  - `test:` Test additions or test framework refactoring
  - `refactor:` Code restructuring without behavior changes
  - `perf:` Performance optimizations

---

## 2. Versioning Scheme

Crysk adheres to **[Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html)** (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`):

- **`MAJOR`**: Breaking changes to CLI behavior, configuration schema, public API exports, or GitHub Actions contracts.
- **`MINOR`**: Backwards-compatible new features, new agent classes, or enhanced tooling.
- **`PATCH`**: Backwards-compatible bug fixes, performance improvements, or documentation updates.

### Version Synchronization Invariant

The project version is maintained in five locations and must always remain identical:

1. `package.json`: `"version": "X.Y.Z"` — the canonical source of truth.
2. `src/index.ts`: `export const ENGINE_VERSION = "X.Y.Z";` — the published API's version constant.
3. `src/assets.ts` (`resolveVersion()`, fallback `return "X.Y.Z";`) — used only when neither the
   compiled `__PRHERO_VERSION__` define nor a readable `package.json` is available.
4. `src/updater.ts` (`detectInstallMethod()`, `options.version ?? "X.Y.Z"`) — the default version
   assumed when no version is passed in.
5. `install.sh` (`VERSION="X.Y.Z"`) — the fallback used when the GitHub API "latest release" lookup
   fails or returns no tag.

`MCP_SERVER_VERSION` in `src/mcp/preflight.ts` is a separate, independent MCP protocol-server version —
it is not part of this invariant and must not be bumped alongside a package release.

### Git Tagging Strategy

Two distinct tag types are used:

1. **Immutable Release Tags (`vX.Y.Z`)**:
   - Annotated Git tags representing specific point-in-time releases (e.g. `v1.0.0`, `v1.1.0`).
   - Once pushed to GitHub, immutable release tags must **never** be moved or re-pointed. The one
     narrow, checked exception is a release run that failed before any GitHub Release existed for the
     tag — see §6, Scenario D. Everything else is a patch release (Scenario A).
2. **Floating Major Tags (`v0`, `v1`, `v2`, etc.)**:
   - Floating tags pointing to the latest release within a major version line. The current floating
     tag is `v0` while the project is pre-1.0 (0.x minor bumps may still break the CLI/config/Action
     contract — see the pre-1.0 semantics note below).
   - Consumed by GitHub Actions users referencing the composite action (e.g., `uses: cryskai/crysk@v0`).
   - Moved/force-updated on every release within that major version line.
   - `v1` is a **frozen legacy tag**: it stopped moving at the last 1.x release (1.1.0) when versions
     were renumbered to 0.x, and must never be moved again. It is kept only so pre-existing workflows
     pinned to `@v1` keep resolving.

### Pre-1.0 semantics (SemVer §4)

While the major version is `0`, a MINOR bump (`0.x.0`) may contain breaking changes to CLI behavior,
configuration schema, or the GitHub Actions contract — SemVer does not guarantee compatibility below
`1.0.0`. Treat every `0.x` release note as "may break" until the project ships `1.0.0` again on its own
merits.

---

## 3. Step-by-Step Release Process

Follow these steps sequentially to execute a release.

### Step 1: Pre-Release Verification

Ensure your local repository is up-to-date with `main` and all verification suites pass:

```bash
# 1. Switch to clean main branch
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# 2. Install dependencies with frozen lockfile
bun install --frozen-lockfile

# 3. Execute test suite, type check, linter, and build bundle
bun test
bun run typecheck
bun run check
bun run build

# 4. (Optional) Run domain-specific probes
bun run fixture-eval
bun run refuter-probe
```

All commands must exit cleanly with code `0`.

**macOS is only tested by `release.yml`.** `ci.yml` runs on `ubuntu-latest` alone, so no pull request ever
runs the suite, the compile or the compiled-binary smoke on darwin; the first time they run is the
release itself (the `0.2.0` release run failed on both macOS legs for exactly this reason). On a Mac,
rehearse that leg before tagging. The empty `HOME` matters: a developer machine with a Claude login hides
tests that silently depend on the macOS keychain.

```bash
# Suite as a bare macOS runner sees it (no keychain item, empty HOME)
env CI=true GITHUB_ACTIONS=true HOME="$(mktemp -d)" bun test

# Compile and smoke the binary exactly as release.yml does (use your own target)
bun build --compile --target=bun-darwin-arm64 --minify --no-compile-autoload-dotenv \
  --no-compile-autoload-bunfig --define __PRHERO_VERSION__='"X.Y.Z"' src/cli.ts \
  --outfile /tmp/crysk-darwin-arm64
bun run scripts/compiled-smoke.ts /tmp/crysk-darwin-arm64
```

### Step 2: Update Changelog

Open `CHANGELOG.md` and prepare the release section:

1. Change `## [Unreleased]` into the new release header: `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` (e.g., `## [1.0.0] - 2026-08-25`).
2. Add a fresh, empty `## [Unreleased]` section above it.
3. Update the link references at the bottom of `CHANGELOG.md`:
   ```markdown
   [Unreleased]: https://github.com/cryskai/crysk/compare/vX.Y.Z...HEAD
   [X.Y.Z]: https://github.com/cryskai/crysk/releases/tag/vX.Y.Z
   ```

### Step 3: Bump Version Numbers

Update the version string in all five synchronization targets:

- In `package.json`:
  ```json
  "version": "X.Y.Z",
  ```
- In `src/index.ts`:
  ```typescript
  export const ENGINE_VERSION = "X.Y.Z";
  ```
- In `src/assets.ts` (`resolveVersion()`'s fallback, used when neither the compiled define nor
  `package.json` is readable):
  ```typescript
  return "X.Y.Z";
  ```
- In `src/updater.ts` (`detectInstallMethod()`'s default when no version is passed in):
  ```typescript
  const version = options.version ?? "X.Y.Z";
  ```
- In `install.sh` (the fallback used when the GitHub API "latest release" lookup fails):
  ```bash
  VERSION="X.Y.Z"
  ```

### Step 4: Commit and Tag Release

The tag you push in the next step MUST carry the exact version you just set in `package.json` (Step 3):
`.github/workflows/release.yml` now runs a `verify-version` job before anything is built that fails the
whole run with `::error::` when `${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}` (the tag, minus its leading `v`) differs from
`package.json`'s `version`. Do the version bump and the changelog heading first, commit, THEN tag —
tagging before bumping the version is exactly the mismatch this guard exists to catch.

Create the release commit and annotate the Git tags:

```bash
# 1. Stage modified files
git add package.json src/index.ts src/assets.ts src/updater.ts install.sh CHANGELOG.md

# 2. Create conventional release commit
git commit -m "chore(release): vX.Y.Z"

# 3. Create immutable annotated tag
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "Release vX.Y.Z"

# 4. Update the floating major tag (v0 while pre-1.0; e.g. v1 once back on a 1.x.y line)
git tag -fa v0 -m "Release v0 (points to vX.Y.Z)"
```

### Step 4b: Publish to npm (manual, before pushing the tag)

`release.yml` publishes to npm only when the `NPM_TOKEN` secret exists, and today it does not. The CI token
failed with `E404` on `PUT /pr-hero`: the `v1.1.0` run created its GitHub Release and the floating tag and
then died at that step, so `1.1.0` never reached npm, and the secret was removed on 2026-09-29. Until npm
trusted publishing is set up, npm is published by hand from the release commit.

Do it **before** pushing the tag. If the publish fails, nothing else has moved; CI used to publish last,
after the GitHub Release, so a failure left a half-release.

```bash
git switch main && git pull --ff-only origin main   # the release commit, clean tree
bun install --frozen-lockfile && bun run build      # the tarball ships dist/
npm login             # interactive (browser or passkey); `npm whoami` fails with E401 without a session
npm whoami            # must print the package owner (see `npm owner ls crysk`)
npm publish --access public
```

- No `--provenance`: it only works from a supported CI provider (OIDC), so a manual publish carries none.
- **Prereleases** (`vX.Y.Z-rc.N`): add `--tag next`. Without it npm points `latest` at the prerelease.
- `npm publish` moves `latest` to the version it publishes, whatever the SemVer order. That is intended for
  the `1.x → 0.x` renumbering (`latest` went from `1.0.0` to `0.2.0`), and it is why an existing `^1` range
  never sees the `0.x` line.
- `E404` on `PUT` for a package that exists means no valid credentials, not a missing package. A
  `PUT ... 202` (see `~/.npm/_logs/*-debug-0.log`) means the registry accepted the upload and is processing
  it asynchronously: for `0.2.0` the version and `latest` took about 9 minutes to appear. Poll, and do not
  publish again:
  ```bash
  until [ "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://registry.npmjs.org/crysk/X.Y.Z)" = 200 ]; do sleep 30; done
  npm view crysk dist-tags --prefer-online   # expect latest: X.Y.Z
  ```
- The workflow's npm step stays in place and is skipped without the secret. If `NPM_TOKEN` is ever restored,
  stop publishing by hand: the step would fail on a version that already exists.

### Step 4c: The rename release (`pr-hero` → `crysk`), one time

The release that carries the rename publishes two packages built from the **same commit**, in this order. This
section describes the sequence; each command is run by the maintainer, never by CI or an agent.

1. **`crysk`** — Step 4b as written: the package whose `package.json` `name` is `crysk`.
2. **One last `pr-hero`** — the same build and the same version, published once more under the old name, so an
   install that runs `npx pr-hero` or `npm i -g pr-hero` lands on a CLI that already reads both the old and the
   new names (markers, `/pr-hero` commands, `PRHERO_*` variables, `~/.prhero`). It must be the full dual-read
   build, not a stub that only prints "renamed": an agent holding an old `pr-hero` cannot parse `<!-- crysk-`
   markers, so the last `pr-hero` the registry serves has to understand them. Only the `name` field differs, set in
   a scratch copy of the package; nothing about it is committed.
3. **`npm deprecate pr-hero "renamed to crysk"`** — after both versions are visible on the registry (Step 5 below,
   NPM Registry Verification), deprecate every `pr-hero` version with that message so `npm install` prints it. No
   further `pr-hero` version is published after this one.

`pr-hero` stays on the registry (an unpublish would break the pinned installs it is meant to carry forward). The GitHub
Release uploads each binary under both names for one version (§4). The repository moved to `cryskai/crysk`;
`juanmaagd/pr-hero` is a mirror kept for workflows and binaries that still name it (Step 4d).

### Step 4d: The repository move (`juanmaagd/pr-hero` → `cryskai/crysk`), one time

GitHub does not guarantee that `uses:` follows a renamed or transferred repository ("GitHub will not redirect
calls to an action hosted by a renamed repository", [Renaming a repository](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/renaming-a-repository)).
So the move keeps a repository at the old name. Each step is run by the maintainer, never by CI or an agent:

1. **Transfer and rename** `juanmaagd/pr-hero` to `cryskai/crysk` (Settings → Transfer, new name `crysk`).
   Issues, pull requests, stars, history, tags, releases, secrets and variables move with it. Check the
   repository's Actions secrets and variables afterwards.
2. **Recreate `juanmaagd/pr-hero` at once** as a public mirror, with **Actions disabled** (`gh api -X PUT
   repos/juanmaagd/pr-hero/actions/permissions -F enabled=false`; the mirror carries `release.yml`, which would
   otherwise start a second release run on every tag pushed there). Then push `main` and every tag,
   so `uses: juanmaagd/pr-hero@v0` (and every `@v0.x.y`) keeps resolving and
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juanmaagd/pr-hero/main/install.sh` keeps serving the installer.
   Creating it stops GitHub's web and git redirect to `cryskai/crysk`: point local clones at the new remote
   (`git remote set-url origin https://github.com/cryskai/crysk.git`).
3. **Every final release while the mirror lives also goes to the mirror.** `release.yml`'s `mirror-legacy` job
   does it after `publish-release`, by running `scripts/mirror-release.sh vX.Y.Z`. The script pushes the release
   commit to the mirror's `main`, pushes `vX.Y.Z` and force-pushes the moved `v0`, copies the GitHub Release with
   the same assets and `SHA256SUMS`, and then verifies the result. It downloads and checks the source assets
   before its first write to the mirror. The floating tag is the release's major (`v0` for 0.x). A binary from
   before the move (`src/updater.ts` read `juanmaagd/pr-hero`) finds its upgrade there; without the mirrored
   release, `pr-hero upgrade` on such a binary reports no new version. Prereleases are not mirrored.
   - The job needs the repository secret `LEGACY_MIRROR_TOKEN`: a fine-grained personal access token of the
     mirror's owner, on `juanmaagd/pr-hero` only, with **Contents** and **Workflows** set to *Read and write*.
     Workflows is required because the pushed commits change `.github/workflows/`, and GitHub refuses such a
     push without it. Without the secret the job fails (after the release is already published): set it and
     re-run the job. Fine-grained tokens expire, so a red `mirror-legacy` on a later release usually means it
     needs renewing.
   - **By hand** (no token, or a failed job): from an up-to-date checkout of `cryskai/crysk`, with `gh` logged in
     as an account that can write the mirror, run `scripts/mirror-release.sh vX.Y.Z`. The script is idempotent:
     a re-run verifies what is already there and changes nothing.
4. Archive the mirror once the version that drops the legacy names ships; an archived repository keeps serving
   its tags.

### Step 5: Push to Remote

Push only after Step 4b succeeded. Pushing the tag starts the release pipeline (§4). Push the release
commit, immutable tag, and updated floating tag to GitHub:

```bash
# 1. Push main branch
git push origin main

# 2. Push the immutable release tag
git push origin vX.Y.Z

# 3. Force-push the floating major tag
git push origin v0 --force
```

---

## 4. Automated CI/CD Release Pipeline

Pushing a `v*` tag automatically triggers the GitHub Actions Release Workflow (`.github/workflows/release.yml`):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Push git tag vX.Y.Z"] --> V["Job: verify-version"]
    V --> B["Job: build-binaries (Matrix)"]
    B --> B1["darwin-arm64 (macOS Apple Silicon)"]
    B --> B2["darwin-x64 (macOS Intel)"]
    B --> B3["linux-x64 (Ubuntu x64)"]
    B --> B4["linux-arm64 (Ubuntu ARM64)"]
    B1 & B2 & B3 & B4 --> C["Upload Binary Artifacts"]
    C --> D["Job: publish-release (Ubuntu)"]
    D --> E["Generate SHA256SUMS"]
    D --> F["Create GitHub Release with Binaries (make_latest: true)"]
    D --> G["Build npm Bundle (bun run build)"]
    D --> H["Publish to NPM (only if NPM_TOKEN is set; skipped today, see Step 4b)"]
```

### Pipeline Workflow Stages

0. **`verify-version`**:
   - Runs first, before anything is built. Compares `${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}` (the pushed tag, minus its
     leading `v`) against `package.json`'s `"version"`. A mismatch fails the job immediately with an
     `::error::` annotation and nothing else in the pipeline runs.
   - WHY this exists: the compiled binary embeds its version from the **tag** (`__PRHERO_VERSION__` in
     the "Compile standalone binary" step below), while `npm publish` ships whatever `package.json` says.
     Those are two independently-settable strings for the same release — without this gate, a tagging
     mistake ships two different version numbers under one release, silently.
1. **`build-binaries`**:
   - Executes across a matrix of 4 runner environments (`macos-latest`, `macos-15-intel`, `ubuntu-latest`, `ubuntu-24.04-arm`), each on its target's own architecture so the smoke below can execute what it built. `fail-fast: false`, so a failing leg does not cancel the other three — they finish and upload, and the run reports every failure rather than only the first. This does **not** keep the release publishing: `publish-release` has a bare `needs: build-binaries`, so any failed leg skips it. That is deliberate — a release missing one platform binary would give `install.sh` a 404 on that architecture, while a failed release leaves the previous version installable.
   - Runs full test suite and typechecks on each OS. This is the only place the suite runs on macOS
     (`ci.yml` is ubuntu-only), so a darwin-only failure surfaces here first; rehearse it in Step 1. A
     failed leg leaves a pushed tag with no release: see §6, Scenario D.
   - Compiles standalone executables using `bun build --compile --minify` with embedded version definitions.
   - **Runs the compiled binary** (`scripts/compiled-smoke.ts`) before uploading it. v1.0.0 shipped a binary whose `review` failed for every user because this step did not exist.
   - Uploads each binary under both names for one version: `crysk-<target>` and a byte-identical `pr-hero-<target>` copy made after the smoke (targets `darwin-arm64`, `darwin-x64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-arm64`). The old name is what an installed `pr-hero upgrade` downloads.
2. **`publish-release`**:
   - Gathers all compiled binaries and computes cryptographic `SHA256SUMS`.
   - Creates a GitHub Release via `softprops/action-gh-release@v2` containing all binaries and checksums,
     with `make_latest: true`. This is explicit rather than left to GitHub's own SemVer-highest default:
     `crysk upgrade` and `install.sh` both resolve GitHub's "latest release", and after the 1.x → 0.x
     renumbering the next release (`0.2.0`) is SemVer-**lower** than the already-published `1.1.0` —
     without `make_latest: true`, GitHub would keep calling `1.1.0` latest forever and every
     upgrade/install would silently stay stuck on the old numbering.
   - Generates release notes automatically from commit history and pull requests.
   - Builds the npm distribution bundle and, **only when the `NPM_TOKEN` secret exists**, publishes it with
     `npm publish --provenance`. The secret is currently unset, so this step is skipped and npm is
     published by hand (Step 4b).

## 5. Post-Release Verification

Perform these sanity checks immediately following a release:

1. **GitHub Release Verification**:
   - Visit `https://github.com/cryskai/crysk/releases/tag/vX.Y.Z`.
   - Confirm all 4 platform binaries and `SHA256SUMS` are attached as release assets, and that the release
     is the one GitHub marks `Latest` (after the renumbering it must not be `1.1.0`):
     ```bash
     gh release view vX.Y.Z --json assets,isPrerelease --jq '.isPrerelease, (.assets[].name)'
     gh release list --limit 3
     ```
   - Confirm the floating tag moved: `git ls-remote origin 'refs/tags/v0^{}'` must equal the release commit.
2. **NPM Registry Verification** (the version can lag the upload by ~10 minutes, see Step 4b; on the rename release also run both commands for `pr-hero`, see Step 4c):
   ```bash
   # Check published package version
   npm view crysk version --prefer-online
   npm view crysk dist-tags --prefer-online
   ```
3. **Installer Script Test**:
   - Test standalone installer download in a temporary environment:
     ```bash
     PRHERO_VERSION="vX.Y.Z" curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cryskai/crysk/main/install.sh | bash
     ~/.crysk/bin/crysk --version   # ~/.prhero/bin/pr-hero on a machine that already had ~/.prhero
     ```
4. **GitHub Action Reference**:
   - Confirm workflows referencing `cryskai/crysk@v0` or `cryskai/crysk@vX.Y.Z` resolve the new
     release. (Workflows still pinned to the frozen `@v1` continue resolving the last 1.x release, by
     design — they receive no further updates.)
5. **Mirror** (while `juanmaagd/pr-hero` lives; final releases only; read-only, after Step 4d.3; the
   `mirror-legacy` job's last step runs the same check, so this repeats it by hand): both tags on
   the mirror point at the release commit, and the mirror's release is `Latest` and carries exactly the assets
   of the `cryskai/crysk` release, byte for byte. Set `V` to the release tag; the block runs in a subshell and
   stops at the first failure without closing your shell:
   ```bash
   ( set -euo pipefail
   V=vX.Y.Z
   COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --verify "$V^{commit}")      # fails here if the tag is missing or V is mistyped
   d=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$d"' EXIT
   for t in v0 "$V"; do                                # annotated tags: compare the commit they point at
     got=$(git ls-remote https://github.com/juanmaagd/pr-hero.git "refs/tags/$t^{}" | cut -f1)
     [ "$got" = "$COMMIT" ] || { echo "mirror $t is '${got:-missing}', expected $COMMIT"; exit 1; }
   done
   gh release list -R juanmaagd/pr-hero --limit 1 | grep -q "$V.*Latest" || { echo "mirror Latest is not $V"; exit 1; }
   gh release download "$V" -R cryskai/crysk -D "$d/new"
   gh release download "$V" -R juanmaagd/pr-hero -D "$d/mirror"
   diff -r "$d/new" "$d/mirror"                        # same file names, same bytes
   (cd "$d/mirror" && shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS)
   [ "$(ls "$d/mirror" | grep -cv '^SHA256SUMS$')" = "$(grep -c . "$d/mirror/SHA256SUMS")" ] \
     || { echo "an asset has no SHA256SUMS line"; exit 1; }
   echo "mirror OK" )
   ```
6. **Doctor Diagnostic**:
   - Run `crysk doctor` locally to verify runtime integrity and toolchain health.

## 6. Rollback & Hotfix Procedures

### Scenario A: Urgent Bug Discovered in Released Version

**Rule: Never mutate existing immutable tags or rewrite release history.**

1. Create a hotfix branch from `main`:
   ```bash
   git checkout -b fix/hotfix-issue-name main
   ```
2. Apply the fix and add regression tests.
3. Update `CHANGELOG.md` with patch notes and increment the patch version (`vX.Y.Z+1`) in `package.json` and `src/index.ts`.
4. Merge into `main` and execute the release process for `vX.Y.Z+1`.
5. The floating `v0` tag will automatically update to point to the new patch release, instantly protecting Action users. (The frozen `v1` tag never moves again — see §2.)

### Scenario B: Compromised or Broken NPM Package

If a critical flaw requires immediately warning package consumers:

1. **Deprecate the flawed version on npm**:
   ```bash
   npm deprecate crysk@X.Y.Z "Critical issue in X.Y.Z; please upgrade to X.Y.Z+1 immediately."
   ```
2. **Unpublishing (Emergency only)**:
   - NPM allows unpublishing only within 72 hours of initial release if no dependents exist (`npm unpublish crysk@X.Y.Z --force`).
   - Prefer deprecation + immediate patch release (`vX.Y.Z+1`) to avoid breaking downstream builds.

### Scenario C: Mispointed Floating Tag

If the floating tag `v0` was pushed to an incorrect commit SHA:

```bash
# Re-align floating tag locally to the correct release commit
git tag -fa v0 <target-commit-sha> -m "Re-align floating v0 tag"

# Force push updated floating tag
git push origin v0 --force
```

Never apply this to `v1` — it is frozen at the last 1.x release and must never be re-pointed.

### Scenario D: Release Run Failed Before the GitHub Release Existed

Typically a `build-binaries` leg failed, so `publish-release` was skipped: the tag is pushed, but there is
no GitHub Release, no binaries and no floating tag. Re-running the failed jobs does not help when the
failure is deterministic, because the run builds the tag's own commit.

The default is still a patch release (Scenario A). Moving the tag is allowed only when **all** of these hold:

1. `gh release view vX.Y.Z` reports `release not found`: nothing consumable hangs off the tag.
2. The fix changes nothing that ships. This must print nothing, and `package.json` must still say `X.Y.Z`
   (if npm was already published, its tarball stays valid because none of its files changed):
   ```bash
   git diff --name-only <old-tag-commit>..origin/main | grep -v '^test/'
   ```
3. The fix reached `main` through the normal pull request flow first.

Then re-point the tag with a lease on its current remote value, so the push fails if anyone touched it in
between. A forced tag update starts a fresh `release.yml` run:

```bash
git fetch origin main
git tag -fa vX.Y.Z -m "Release vX.Y.Z" origin/main
git push origin vX.Y.Z --force-with-lease=refs/tags/vX.Y.Z:$(git ls-remote origin refs/tags/vX.Y.Z | cut -f1)
```

Record the deviation in the promotion pull request. Precedent: `v0.2.0` moved from `d36e51a` to `05feaac`
on 2026-09-29 after five keychain-dependent tests failed on both macOS legs (fixed test-only).

name: pr-hero-consolidator
description: Post-refuter pass that merges findings stating the same defect and splits asides, so each posted comment states one defect.
model: sonnet
effort: high
---
You consolidate the findings a code reviewer is about to post on one pull request, so that every posted comment states exactly ONE defect.

You receive the findings as JSON: id, path, line, severity, hunter, claim. You have no tools and no code: work only from the claims.

Do exactly two things.

1. Merge findings that describe the same defect: the same root cause reported by two hunters, or the same mistake repeated at sibling sites (a copied pattern in two files, the same bundle edited twice). Merged findings become one output finding whose claim states the defect once and names every site. Findings that merely touch the same code, or the same function, but describe different defects are NOT merged.

2. Split asides. A claim sometimes carries a second issue after "Separately", "Also", "In addition", "The test also", or a trailing list. If that aside names a distinct defect (a different wrong behaviour, with its own location or mechanism), move it to its own output finding. If it is only commentary, a consequence of the main defect, a style or test-hygiene remark, or a suggestion, delete it.

Rules:
- Never add a defect that is not in the input claims. Never judge whether a defect is correct, likely or important: step 2 deletes an aside only when it does not name a distinct defect, never because the defect it names looks minor or doubtful. Never drop a whole finding: every input id must appear in the sources of at least one output finding.
- Keep the reviewer's wording. Copy sentences; trim them; do not paraphrase into something new. Keep code identifiers, line references and the concrete consequence.
- Each output claim states one defect, its mechanism, and its consequence, in at most about 120 words.
- For a merge, "primary" is the most severe source (BLOCKER > CRITICAL > WARNING > SUGGESTION), ties broken by the first in input order. For a split aside, "primary" is the finding it came from and "split" is true.

Final message: exactly one JSON object, no prose, no code fences:
{"findings":[{"primary":"F001","sources":["F001","F004"],"split":false,"claim":"..."}]}
